To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

free fatty acids activate a previously unrecognized Ca(2+):H+ antiporter in yeast mitochondria, that this antiporter is responsible for a futile cycle of calcium accumulation and release in the presence of exogenous calcium and ETH129, that this futile cycle can be corrected by the addition of albumin or EGTA, and that the antiporter is inactivated by the degradation of phospholipids that occurs in isolated mitochondria.
yeast mitochondria have an active Ca2+:2 H+ antiporter, and that free fatty acids stimulate this activity.

yeast mitochondria have a previously unrecognized Ca(2+):2H(+) antiporter that is activated by free fatty acids, that the antiporter is the cause of a futile cycle of mitochondrial Ca(2+) accumulation and release, and that the antiporter activity is a result of the hydrolysis by yeast mitochondria of their phospholipid constituents.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of free fatty acids on yeast mitochondria.
the regulation of the Ca2+:2+H+ antiporter in yeast mitochondria, which is shown to be a previously unrecognized and highly active system.

the behavior of Ca2+:2Na+ and Ca2+:2K+ antiports in mitochondria from different sources, with the behavior of a Ca2+:2Cl– antiporter in yeast mitochondria, with the behavior and regulation of a Ca2+–activated H+ conductance in the inner membrane, and with the regulation of the mitochondrial phospholipid pool.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
free fatty acids activate an antiporter that mediates a futile cycle of H+ and Ca2+ transport.

free fatty acids activate a vigorous Ca2+:2+H+ antiport activity in yeast mitochondria, and that this antiporter, when activated, leads to futile cycles of Ca2+ transport when exogenous Ca+ and the mitochondrial uncoupler ETH 129 are present.
yeast mitochondria have been shown to contain a Ca2+:2 H+ antiporter that can operate in a Ca2+-free system and that can be activated by the presence of free long-chain fatty acids.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the Ca2+ permeability of yeast mitochondria can be increased severalfold in the presence of ETH 129, but that the extent of this increase is highly variable, and is dependent on the presence of fatty acids in the medium.

yeast mitochondria have a Ca2+-dependent phospholipase A2 activity, that this activity leads to the formation of free fatty acids that activate a Ca2+:2 H+ antiporter, and that this antiporter is responsible for a futile cycle of mitochondrial Ca2+ transport when exogenous Ca+2 and ETH 129are present.

the Ca2+–dependent permeability transition in yeast mitochondria, like its counterpart in rat liver mitochondria, is not a simple event but is a complex process involving the concerted action of several different activities, including a Ca2+–induced Ca2+ release activity, a Ca2+ uniporter, a Ca2+:2 H+ antiporter, a fatty acid-dependent Ca2+–H+ antiporter, and a phospholipase A1/A2.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the Ca2+:2 H+ antiporter is highly active in yeast mitochondria, and that this activity is regulated by the presence of free long chain fatty acids in the medium.
yeast mitochondria have a previously unrecognized Ca(2+):2H(+) antiporter that is activated by fatty acids.
the Ca2+ retention and release cycle in yeast is not a passive process, but is actively regulated by an antiport system.
